Elham is a young, unmarried author — likely a Muslimah — who crossed into this other realm through a Fall: she went to sleep and her mind and body crossed over entirely into the reality she believed she had only been imagining. What she took to be creative inspiration turns out to have been something that activated when she became an Author, granting her accurate, intimate knowledge of real events and real people in this realm. She is the most recent in a line of Authors who have chronicled this world's true happenings, which makes her knowledge both extraordinary and acutely dangerous. Now she finds herself early in the story inside the main antagonist's domain — a figure whose name the notes place somewhere in the territory of "Silver" and "Heart," and who reads less like a traditional mafia don and more like a farther-reaching version of Inkheart's Capricorn: dangerous, broad in influence, and not entirely without some inner dimension that Elham knows about without having earned the right to know it. That unearned intimacy is precisely what makes her presence so precarious. The Sparrow, this antagonist's right-hand man, brought her there — he came to her with something she needed, and his method is characteristically his own: he takes people under his wing not through force but through comfort and contingency, offering shelter and provision in exchange for loyalty over time.

She cannot simply leave. Humans in this realm are registered — not always out of malice, but the effect is the same as well-meaning surveillance — and any human who appears without being logged draws immediate attention. Slipping out too quickly risks unmasking her as both human and Author, a combination that could make her a target of the antagonist she already knows too well, or an uncomfortable figure even to the story's hero, given how personally Authors tend to write about their subjects. The notes are careful to note that her anxiety is at least partly paranoia, but she is equally clear-eyed that the threat of exposure is real the moment she makes a wrong move. The task she is sitting with, then, is finding a way out of that domain without triggering the very discovery she is trying to avoid.

— From your notes only. Nothing invented.
